blocks.html: 5 Duality

This exposé contains a few theorems and compatibilities, all relating to Poincaré duality. In section 1, the local biduality theorem in dimension \(1\) [21] and a few calculations of two. In section 2, a very economical proof of Poincaré duality on curves, which M. Artin taught me. In section 3, a compatibility linking two definitions of the pairing that gives rise to Poincaré duality for curves: by cup-product, or by self-duality of the Jacobian. In section 4, finally, the proof of the compatibility of the title.
Throughout the exposé, the schemes will be noetherian and separated, and \(n\) is an integer invertible on all the schemes considered.
1 Local biduality, in dimension \(1\)

Let \(S\) be a regular scheme purely of dimension \(1\). We propose to show that the complex reduced to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) in degree \(0\) is dualizing, i.e. that for \(\mathscr{K}\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_c^b(S,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) (\((-)_c\) for constructible), if we set \(D\mathscr{K}=\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathscr{K},\mathbb{Z}/n)\), then \(D\mathscr{K}\) is again constructible with bounded cohomology, and that the canonical morphism \(\alpha\) from \(\mathscr{K}\) to \(D D\mathscr{K}\) is an isomorphism.
For \(\mathscr{K}\) in \(\mathsf{D}^-\), and \(\mathscr{L}\) arbitrary, we have
\[ \hom(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{L},\mathbb{Z}/n) = \hom(\mathscr{L},\operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{K},\mathbb{Z}/n)) \text{.} \]

The morphism from \(\mathscr{K}\) to \(DD\mathscr{K}\) is defined assuming \(D\mathscr{K}\) in \(\mathsf{D}^-\); if \(\beta:D\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathscr{K}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\) is the canonical pairing, it is defined by the pairing \(\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} D\mathscr{K}=D\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathscr{K} \xrightarrow{\beta} \mathbb{Z}/n\).

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) be a separated morphism of finite type. Set \(\mathscr{K}_X=\mathsf{R} f^!\mathbb{Z}/n\). For \(\mathscr{K}\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}^-(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), we set \(D\mathscr{K} = \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathscr{K},\mathscr{K}_X)\). The adjunction between \(\mathsf{R} f_!\) and \(\mathsf{R} f^!\) ensures that

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} \mathsf{R} f_\ast D\mathscr{K} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_! (\mathscr{K}\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} D\mathscr{K}) \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} f_! \mathsf{R} f^! \mathbb{Z}/n \ar[r] & \mathbb{Z}/n . } \]
The symmetry of this description shows that, for \(f\) proper, the diagram

\[ \tag{1.2.1} \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{K} \ar[r] \ar[d] & D D \mathsf{R} f_\ast \mathscr{K} \ar[d]^-\wr \\ \mathsf{R} f_\ast D D \mathscr{K} \ar[r]^\sim & D\mathsf{R} f_\ast D\mathscr{K} } \]
is commutative.

If \(f\) is the inclusion of a closed point, we know that \(\mathsf{R} f^!\mathbb{Z}/n=\mathbb{Z}/n(-1)[-2]\) – that is, up to a twist and a shift, \(\mathbb{Z}/n\). Over the spectrum of a field, this complex is dualizing (Pontryagin duality for \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules). By (1.2.1), we thus have \(\mathscr{K}\xrightarrow{\sim} D D\mathscr{K}\) for \(\mathscr{K}\) of the form \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathscr{L}\) – and hence when the support of \(\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^\bullet(\mathscr{K})\) is finite.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.3

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow S\) be a dense open of \(S\) and \(\mathscr{F}\) a locally constant constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules on \(U\). We have \(\mathsf{D} j_\ast \mathscr{F} = j_\ast D \mathscr{F}\), i.e. \(\operatorname{Hom}(j_\ast \mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/n) = j_\ast\operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/n)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(j_\ast\mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/n) = 0\) for \(i>0\).

On \(U\), \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(j_\ast\mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/n)=0\) for \(i>0\), since \(\mathscr{F}\) is locally constant (and \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) is an injective \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-module), while for \(i=0\) it is the dual \(\mathscr{F}^\vee\) of \(\mathscr{F}\). We check that \(\hom(j_\ast\mathscr{F},\mathbb{Z}/n)=j_\ast\mathscr{F}^\vee\), and it remains to check the vanishing of the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\) (\(i>0\)) at the points of \(S\setminus U\). The problem is local at these points. This reduces us to assuming that \(S\) is a strictly local trait and that \(U\) is reduced to its generic point \(\eta\). Let \(I=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\eta}/\eta)\). The sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) is identified with the Galois module \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}\), and the special fibre of \(j_\ast \mathscr{F}\) with \(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\).
Let \(i\) be the inclusion of the closed point \(s\), and let us apply \(D\) to the exact sequences

\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & j_! \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & j_\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & i_\ast \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I \ar[r] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & j_! \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I \ar[r] \ar[u] & \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I \ar[r] \ar[u] & i_\ast \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I \ar[r] \ar[u] & 0 . } \]
We obtain a morphism of triangles

\[ \xymatrix{ i_\ast\left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee (-1)[-2] \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & D j_\ast\mathscr{F} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathscr{F}^\vee \ar[d] \\ i_\ast\left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee(-1)[-2] \ar[r] & \left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} j_\ast \mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I . } \]
The long exact sequence deduced from the first row yields the vanishing of the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\) (\(i>2\)) and, taking the fibre at \(s\), we find

\[ \xymatrix@=0.7cm{ 0 \ar[r] & \left(\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^1(D j_\ast\mathscr{F}\right)_s \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(I,\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^\vee\right) \ar[r]^-\partial \ar[d] & \left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee(-1) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & \left(\underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^2 D j_\ast\mathscr{F}\right)_s \ar[r] & 0 \\ & 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(I,(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I)^\vee\right) \ar[r]^-\partial & \left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee(-1) \ar[r] & 0 . } \]
Since \(\left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^I\right)^\vee = \left(\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^\vee\right)_I\), setting \(M=\mathscr{F}_{\overline{\eta}}^\vee\), it finally remains to check that
\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(I,M) \ar[r]^-\sim & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(I,M_I) . } \]

If \(p\) is the residue characteristic exponent, \(I\) is an extension of a group isomorphic to \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{p'} = \varprojlim_{(m,p)=1} \mathbb{Z}/m\) by a \(p\)-group \(P\). Since \(P\) is prime to the order of \(M\), we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(P,M)=0\) (\(i>0\)) and \((M_I)^P=(M^P)_I\). This allows us to replace \(M\) by \(M^P\) and \(I\) by \(I/P\). Finally, we have a functorial isomorphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{p'},M)\sim (\)coinvariants of \(\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{p'}\), in \(M)\), whence the theorem.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.4

For \(\mathscr{K}\in \operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_c^b(S,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), we have \(\mathscr{K}\xrightarrow{\sim} D D \mathscr{K}\).

By dévissage, we reduce to assuming that \(\mathscr{K}\) is reduced to a constructible sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\) in degree \(0\), and that \(\mathscr{F}\) is either of finite support (1.2), or of the form \(j_\ast\mathscr{F}_1\) as in 1.3. In this second case, 1.3 reduces us to local biduality for \(\mathscr{F}\) locally constant on \(U\).

pages.title: Poincaré duality for curves, after M. Artin

blocks.html: 2 Poincaré duality for curves, after M. Artin

Let \(X\) be a projective smooth curve over \(k\) algebraically closed. We set \(\mathscr{K}_X=\mathbb{Z}/n(1)[2]\) and, for \(\mathscr{K}\in\operatorname{Ob} \mathsf{D}_c^b(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), \(D\mathscr{K}=\mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathscr{K},\mathscr{K}_X)\). For \(M\) a \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-module, we also set \(D M = \hom(M,\mathbb{Z}/n)\); likewise for complexes of modules. The trace morphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{K}_X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), or \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K}_X)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), defines a pairing \(\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K})\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes}\mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,D\mathscr{K}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\). Poincaré duality between cohomology and cohomology with proper supports of an open \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) of \(X\) says that, for \(\mathscr{K}=j_!\mathbb{Z}/n\), this pairing identifies each factor with the dual of the other.
I present below a proof, communicated to me by M. Artin, that for \(\mathscr{K}\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathsf{D}_c^b(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\), this pairing is always perfect, i.e. defines an isomorphism
\[ \tag{2.1.1} \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,\mathscr{K}) \ar[r]^-\sim & D \mathsf{R}\Gamma(X,D\mathscr{K}) . } \]
For every constructible sheaf \(\mathscr{F}\), let us set
\[ '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) = \mathbb{Z}/n \text{-dual of } \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{-i}(X,D\mathscr{F}) \text{.} \]
That (2.1.1) be an isomorphism is equivalent to the following theorem.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.2

For \(\mathscr{F}\) a constructible sheaf of \(\mathbb{Z}/n\)-modules, we have

\[ \tag{2.2.1} \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r]^-\sim & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) . } \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3

Let \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) be a generically étale morphism between smooth curves over \(k\). We have \(\mathscr{K}_X=f^\ast\mathscr{K}_Y=\mathsf{R} f^!\mathscr{K}_Y\), with \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) as adjunction arrow \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathsf{R} f^!\mathscr{K}_Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{K}_Y\).

We reduce to checking that for \(f\) finite, we have that \(f_\ast \mathsf{R} f^!\mathscr{K}_Y = \mathsf{R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n,\mathscr{K}_Y)\) is \(f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n\), with \(\operatorname{tr}_f\) as adjunction arrow. The vanishing of the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\) (\(i>0\)) follows from 1.3, and the assertion follows.

We may say, more explicitly, that \(\mathsf{R} f^!\) is the derived functor of the functor \(f^!:f^!\mathscr{F}(U)=\hom(f_!\mathbb{Z}_U,\mathscr{F})\) and 1.3 implies the vanishing of the \(\mathsf{R}^i f^!\mathbb{Z}/n\) for \(i>0\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Let \(f:X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) be a generically étale morphism of projective smooth curves over \(k\). We have \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,f_\ast \mathscr{F})='\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X',\mathscr{F})\); this isomorphism is functorial and the diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,f_\ast\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,f_\ast\mathscr{F}) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X',\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X',\mathscr{F}) } \]

is commutative.
The isomorphism is given by 1.2: \(D f_\ast\mathscr{F}=f_\ast D\mathscr{F}\).

Let us prove 2.2. If \(\mathscr{F}\) is reduced to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\) at a point, extended by \(0\), we have \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(D\mathscr{F}) = \operatorname{Ext}^\bullet(\mathscr{F},\mathscr{K}_X)=\mathbb{Z}/n\) in degree \(0\), and in the pairing \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\mathscr{F})\otimes\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(D\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), we have \(1\otimes 1\mapsto 1\) ([IV]Cycle, 2.1.5): the duality is perfect. The case where \(\mathscr{F}\) has finite support is treated in the same way.
For \(\mathscr{F}\) an arbitrary constructible sheaf, \(\mathscr{A}\) the subsheaf of its sections with finite support, and \(\mathscr{G}=\mathscr{F}/\mathscr{A}\), the exact sequence
\[ \tag{2.5.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{A} \ar[r] & \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & 0 } \]
yields a diagram

\[ \tag{2.5.2} \xymatrix@=.5cm{ & & 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{A}) \ar[r] \ar[d]^-\wr & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{-1}(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^{-1}(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{A}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{F}) \ar[r] & 0 } \]

and compatible isomorphisms \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F})\xrightarrow{\sim} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{G})\), \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \xrightarrow{\sim} '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{G})\) (\(i\ne 0,-1\)). If \(j:U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) is an open on which \(\mathscr{F}\) is locally constant, we have an exact sequence
\[ \tag{2.5.3} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & j_\ast j^\ast \mathscr{F} \ar[r] & \mathscr{B} \ar[r] & 0 } \]

with \(\mathscr{B}\) of finite support. Since \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,j_\ast j^\ast\mathscr{F}) = D \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{2-i} (X,j_\ast(j^\ast\mathscr{F})^\vee(1))\) by 1.3, this \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i=0\) for \(i<0\), and (2.5.2) and the long exact sequence defined by (2.5.3) show that \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\) is always zero for \(i<0\).

If \(\mathscr{F}=\mathbb{Z}/n\), the theorem is true for \(i=0\) and \(2\). This expresses that, for \(X\) connected, the trace morphism \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{Z}/n\) is an isomorphism. By 2.4, the theorem remains true for \(i=0\) and \(\mathscr{F}=f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n\).

For \(\mathscr{F}\) again arbitrary and \(\mathscr{G}\) as above, there exists \(f:X'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) as in 2.4 such that \(\mathscr{G}\) embeds in \(f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n\):
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n \ar[r] & \mathscr{Q} \ar[r] & 0 . } \]

Changing \(X'\) to an \(X''/X'\), we may assume that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,\mathscr{F}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X,f_\ast\mathbb{Z}/n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X',\mathbb{Z}/n)\) is zero for \(i>0\). Let us then consider

\[ \xymatrix@=.3cm{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(S',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] \ar[d]^-\wr & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{Q}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r]^-0 \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{Q}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \cdots \\ 0 \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{Q}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G}) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] & '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{Q}) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

The isomorphism at \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X')\) yields \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G})\hookrightarrow '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathscr{G})\), and the same injectivity for \(\mathscr{F}\) (2.5.2). Applied to \(\mathscr{Q}\), this gives \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G})\hookrightarrow '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G})\). We apply this to \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X',\mathbb{Z}/n)\). This group having the same order as \('\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X',\mathbb{Z}/n)=D(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X',\mathbb{Z}/n)(1))\), we find an isomorphism, and \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G}) \xrightarrow{\sim} '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{G})\). Likewise for \(\mathscr{F}\). For \(i=2\), we already know that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X',\mathbb{Z}/n) \xrightarrow{\sim} '\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X',\mathbb{Z}/n)\), and we proceed in the same way, then stop, for lack of combatants.
3 Poincaré duality for curves
In this section, we prove the compatibility ([I]Arcata 6.2.2.3).

The notations are those of ([I]Arcata 6.2.3): \(\overline{X}\) is a projective, smooth, and connected curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), \(D\) is a reduced divisor on \(\overline{X}\), \(0\) a point of \(X=\overline{X}\setminus D\)
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar@{^{(}->}[r]^-j & \overline{X} & D , \ar[l]_-i} \]

and \(\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X},_D\mathbb{G}_m)\) where \(_D\mathbb{G}_m\) is the sheaf of sections of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) congruent to \(1\mod D\). We recall that \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n\), and that \(x\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{O}(x)\) defines a canonical map \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})\). We set \(f_0(x)=f(x)-f(0):X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\).

Let us again denote by \(j\) the inclusion of \(X\times X\) in \(X\times \overline{X}\). The diagonal \(\Delta\) of \(X\times X\) is closed in \(X\times \overline{X}\); it defines a class in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_\Delta^2(X\times X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)=\underline{\operatorname{H}}_\Delta^2(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\). We denote by \(c\) its image in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\).
The Künneth formula ensures that

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(\overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^\bullet(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \text{.} \]
We propose to compute the \((1,1)\)-component of \(c\),

\[ c^{1,1} \in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1\left(X,\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n\right) \text{.} \]
The exact sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r]^n & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r] & 0 } \]

makes \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\) a \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n\)-torsor over \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\). Let us denote by \(u\) the class, in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n))=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})_n)\), of its inverse image under \(f_0\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

With the preceding notations, \(c^{1,1}=-u\).

Let \(e\) be the difference of the images in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) of the cohomology classes of \(\Delta\) and \(X\times\{0\}\) being of Künneth type \((0,2)\), we have \(c^{1,1}=e^{1,1}\). Consider the Leray spectral sequence for \(\mathrm{pr}_1:X\times \overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) and the sheaf \(j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\):

\[ E_2^{pq} = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X,\mathsf{R}^q {\mathrm{pr}_1}_\ast j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^p(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^q(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)) \Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{H}}^{p+q}(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \text{.} \]

It degenerates: it is the tensor product of \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^\bullet(X)\) with the (trivial) Leray spectral sequence for \(\overline{X}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) and the sheaf \(j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\). The divisor \(\Delta-X\times\{0\}\) is fibre by fibre of degree \(0\), so that the image of \(e\) in \(E^{02}\) is zero. We may thus speak of its image \(\overline{e}\) in \(E^{1,1}\), and we must show that \(\overline{e} = -u\).

Let \(\mathscr{G}\) on \(X\times\overline{X}\) be the subsheaf of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) formed by the local sections whose restriction to the subscheme \(X\times D\) is \(1\). We again have an exact sequence
\[ \tag{3.2.1} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & \mathscr{G} \ar[r] & 0 } \]

and \(e\) is the image under \(\partial\) of the class \(e_1\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X\times\overline{X},\mathscr{G})\) of the invertible sheaf \(\mathscr{O}(\Delta-X\times\{0\})\) trivialized by \(1\) on \(X\times D\).
The direct image under \(\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast}\) of the distinguished triangle defined by (2.2.1) is a distinguished triangle

\[ \tag{3.2.2} \xymatrix{ & \ar[r]^-\partial & \mathsf{R} \mathrm{pr}_{1\ast} j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} \mathrm{pr}_{2\ast}\mathscr{G} \ar[r] & \mathsf{R} \mathrm{pr}_{2\ast}\mathscr{G} \ar[r]^-\partial & } \]
and the diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X\times \overline{X},\mathscr{G}) \ar[r]^-\partial \ar@{=}[d]^-{(1)} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar@{=}[d] \\ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast} \mathscr{G}) \ar[r]^-\partial & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast} j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) } \]

is commutative: our problem becomes that of identifying the image in \(E^{11}=\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n))\) (the image in \(E^{02}\) being zero) of the image under \(\partial_{\text{(3.2.2)}}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast}\mathscr{G}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X,\mathsf{R}\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast} j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) of the class, again denoted \(e_1\), which corresponds to \(e_1\) by (1).

The sheaf \(\mathsf{R}^1\mathrm{pr}_{1\ast}\mathscr{G}\) is defined by the group scheme over \(X\) that is the inverse image of the algebraic group \(\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})\) over \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), and the image of \(e_1\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\mathsf{R}^1\mathrm{pr}_\ast\mathscr{G}) = \hom(X,\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X}))\) is \(f_0\).
Let us represent the triangle (3.2.2) as defined by a short exact sequence of complexes of sheaves.
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{A} \ar[r] & \mathscr{B} \ar[r] & \mathscr{C} \ar[r] & 0 . } \]
Let \(\mathscr{B}'\) be the subsheaf of

\[ \tau_{\leqslant 1} \mathscr{B} : \cdots \mathscr{B}^0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \ker(d) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \cdots \]

obtained by replacing \({\mathscr{B}'}^1=\ker(d)\) by the inverse image, under \(\ker(d)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\underline{\operatorname{H}}}^1(\mathscr{B}) = \operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X})\) over \(X\), of \(\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})\) over \(X\). Let \(\mathscr{A}'=\mathscr{A}\cap \mathscr{B}'\) and \(\mathscr{C}'\) be the image of \(\mathscr{B}'\). We have \(\mathscr{A}'=\tau_{\leqslant 1}(\mathscr{A})\), and \(\mathscr{C}'\) is deduced from \(\mathscr{C}\) as \(\mathscr{B}'\) from \(\mathscr{B}\), whence a commutative diagram of short exact sequences

\[ \tag{3.2.3} \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \mathscr{A} \ar[r] & \mathscr{B} \ar[r] & \mathscr{C} \ar[r] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \tau_{\leqslant 1} \mathscr{A} \ar[r] \ar[u] \ar[d] & \mathscr{B}' \ar[r] \ar[u] \ar[d] & \mathscr{C}' \ar[r] \ar[u] \ar[d] & 0 \\ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)[1] \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})[1] \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X})[1] \ar[r] & 0 } \]
where the last row must be viewed as an exact sequence of complexes of sheaves concentrated in degree \(1\) on \(X\).

1. \(e\in \mathsf{H}^2(X,\mathscr{A})\) comes from \(\widetilde e\in \mathsf{H}^2(X,\tau_{\leqslant 1}\mathscr{A})\) (since its image in \(E^{02}\) is zero). We seek the image \(\overline{e}\) of \(\widetilde e\) in \(\mathsf{H}^2(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)[-1]) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n))\).

  2. \(e_1\in \mathsf{H}^1(X,\mathscr{C})\) comes from \(\widetilde e_1\in \mathsf{H}^1(X,\mathscr{C}')\), since its image \(f_0\) in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\operatorname{Pic}_D(\overline{X}))\) lies in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X,\operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}))\). We may take \(\widetilde e=\partial \widetilde e_1\).

  3. We thus have \(\overline{e} = \partial f_0\), where \(\partial \) is defined by (3.2.2), and where we use the usual isomorphisms \(\mathsf{H}^2(X,\mathscr{F}[-1]) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathscr{F})\). These isomorphisms anticommute with \(\partial\), so that \(\overline{e}=-\partial f_0\), for \(\partial\) defined by the exact sequence

    \[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Pic}_D^0(\overline{X}) \ar[r] & 0 } \]

    We conclude by ([IV]Cycles, 1.1.1).

For every homomorphism \(\varphi:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\), let \(\varphi(u)\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\) be the image of \(u\) under \(\varphi:\underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\). If \(x\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\), the cup-product \(\varphi(u)\smallsmile x\) is in \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\). We propose to prove that

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4

\(\operatorname{tr}(\varphi(u)\smallsmile x) = \varphi(x)\).
This identity is deduced, by applying \(\varphi\), from
\[ \tag{3.4.1} \operatorname{tr}(u\smallsmile x) = x \]
where \(\operatorname{tr}\) is this time the map

\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{tr}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\otimes\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) , } \]
so that \(x\mapsto \operatorname{tr}(u\smallsmile x)\) is the composite map

\[ \tag{3.4.2} \begin{aligned} &\xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-{u\otimes x} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[l]_-\sim} \\ &\xymatrix{ \ar[r]^-{(1)} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[r]^-{\operatorname{tr}\otimes\operatorname{id}} & \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) } \end{aligned} \]
where (1) is given by \(a\otimes b\otimes c\mapsto (a\smallsmile c)\otimes b\).

Let us express this morphism in terms of the trace morphism \(\operatorname{tr}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^3(X\times X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n^{\otimes 2}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) relative to the second projection. For \(x\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^3\), \(\operatorname{tr}(x)\) is computed as follows: of its Künneth components, we keep only the one of type \((2,1)\), and we apply \(\operatorname{tr}:\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^2(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{Z}/n\).
Let us denote by \(u'\) the image of \(u\) under the map

\begin{align*} &\xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)) & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) = \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/n)\otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \ar[l]_-\sim} \\ &\xymatrix{ \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X\times \overline{X},\mathbb{Z}/n\boxtimes j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) . } \end{align*}
In view of the relation between Künneth and cup-product, we have
\[ \operatorname{tr}(u\smallsmile x) = -\operatorname{tr}(u'\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x) \text{.} \]
The second cup-product is that of ([IV]Cycle 1.2.4):

\[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^2(X\times \overline{X},\mathbb{Z}/n\boxtimes j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) \otimes \underline{\operatorname{H}}^1(\overline{X}\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n\boxtimes \mathbb{Z}/n) \ar[r] & \underline{\operatorname{H}}^3(\overline{X}\times \overline{X},j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n \boxtimes j_!\boldsymbol{\mu}_n) . } \]

The sign – comes from the permutation of two symbols of degree \(1\) in (1). Since \(c\smallsmile\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x\) and \(c^{1,1}\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast\) have the same \((2,1)\)-Künneth component, and since \(u'=c^{1,1}\), we have
\[ \operatorname{tr}(u\smallsmile x) = \operatorname{tr}(c\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x) \text{.} \]

The cup-product on the right can this time be interpreted as the cup-product ([IV]Cycle 1.2.5) of \(\operatorname{cl}(\Delta)\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_\Delta^2(X\times X,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\) with \(\mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x\in \underline{\operatorname{H}}_c^1(\Delta,\boldsymbol{\mu}_n)\). On \(\Delta\), we have \(\mathrm{pr}_1=\mathrm{pr}_2\), whence

\[ \operatorname{tr}(c\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x) = \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{cl}(\Delta)\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_1^\ast x) = \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{cl}(\Delta)\smallsmile \mathrm{pr}_2^\ast x) = \operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{cl}(\Delta))\smallsmile x = x \text{.} \]
4 Compatibility SGA 4 XVIII 3.1.10.3

In [2], in the grip of discouragement, I did not check the compatibility of the title. Although it turns out to be nothing but smoke, I feel bound to remedy this gap here. For \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\) separated of finite type, it was a matter of checking that the adjunction morphism \(\mathsf{R} f_!\mathsf{R} f^!\mathscr{L}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{L}\) is compatible with every étale localization \(k:V\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} S\). Denoting by \(k\) and \(f\) several arrows, as below, we must check a commutativity:

\[ \xymatrix{ X_V \ar[r]^-k \ar[d]^-f & X \ar[d]^-f \\ V \ar[r]^-k & S } \qquad \xymatrix{ k^\ast \mathsf{R} f_! \mathsf{R} f^!\mathscr{L} \ar[r]^-{k^\ast(\text{adj})} \ar[d]^-\sim & k^\ast \mathscr{L} \ar@{=}[d] \\ \mathsf{R} f_! \mathsf{R} f^! k^\ast \mathscr{L} \ar[r]^-{\text{adj}} & k^\ast \mathscr{L} . } \]
At the level of complexes, the desired commutativity reads (loc. cit.)
\[ \xymatrix{ k^\ast f_!^\bullet f^!_\bullet \mathscr{L} \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{(1)} & k^\ast \mathscr{L} \ar@{=}[d] \\ f_!^\bullet f^!_\bullet k^\ast \mathscr{L} \ar[r] & k^\ast \mathscr{L} . } \]

One checks it component by component, which reduces to a compatibility for \(\mathscr{L}\) a sheaf and for each of the pairs of adjoint functors \((f_i^!,f_!^i)\), denoted simply \(f^!\) and \(f_!\). The arrow (1) is defined from the isomorphism \((2):k^\ast f_!=f_! k^\ast\), and from a morphism \((3):k^\ast f^! \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f^! k^\ast\) that is deduced from it. In loc. cit., one introduces first a morphism \((4):k_! f_!\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f_! k_!\), deduced from \((2)\) by adjunction of \(k^\ast=k^!\) and of \(k_!:k_! f_!\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_! f_! k^\ast k_!\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} k_! k^\ast f_! k_! \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f_! k_!\), and one deduces \((3)\) from \((4)\) by adjunction. It comes to the same thing to deduce \((3)\) from \((2)\) by adjunction of \(f_!\) and \(f^!:k^\ast \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f^! f_! k^\ast f^!\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f^! k^\ast f_! f^! \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f^! k^\ast\).
Writing \(k\) for \(k^\ast\) and omitting \(\mathscr{L}\), the commutativity is then that of the outer boundary of

\[ \xymatrix@=.5cm{ k f_! f^! \ar[r] \ar@{=}[d] & f_! k f^! \ar[r] & f_! f^! f_! k f^! \ar[r] & f_! f^! k f_! f^! \ar@{=}[d] \\ k f_! f^! \ar[d] & & & f_! f^! k f_! f^! \ar[d] \ar[lll]\\ k & & & f_! f^! k . \ar[lll]} \]

In the first row, one finds a homomorphism \(k _! f^! \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} f_! f^! k f_! f^!\), defined because \(k f_! f^!\) is of the form \(f_! X\) (\(X=k f^!\)); it has as retraction the adjunction morphism in the second row, and the commutativity of the lower square expresses the functoriality of this adjunction morphism.
